warmup.q: transfer(from, to) locks from, then to. One thread runs transfer(a, b) while another runs transfer(b, a), many times. What is the worst that can happen?
options: A few transfers run slower because of contention
Money is lost, because the two transfers race on the balances
Both threads stop for good, each holding one lock and waiting for the other
The JVM detects the problem and throws a DeadlockException
warmup.why: If each thread takes its first lock before the other takes its second, T1 holds a and waits for b while T2 holds b and waits for a. Neither can ever move. The balances stay correct, since the locks still exclude, but nothing progresses. Java has no DeadlockException: the threads just sit there, BLOCKED, until the process is restarted.

sections.h: Two locks taken in opposite orders can stop forever
sections.html:
Here is a transfer that looks careful. It locks both accounts, so the debit and the credit happen as one step:

Java
void transfer(Account from, Account to, long cents) {
    synchronized (from) {
        synchronized (to) {
            from.debit(cents);
            to.credit(cents);
        }
    }
}
// thread 1: transfer(a, b, 100)        thread 2: transfer(b, a, 50)
Kotlin
fun transfer(from: Account, to: Account, cents: Long) {
    synchronized(from) {
        synchronized(to) {
            from.debit(cents)
            to.credit(cents)
        }
    }
}
// thread 1: transfer(a, b, 100)        thread 2: transfer(b, a, 50)

Each call is correct on its own. Together they can freeze. Thread 1 locks a. Before it locks b, thread 2 locks b. Now thread 1 waits for b, which thread 2 holds, and thread 2 waits for a, which thread 1 holds. Neither will ever let go, because each releases its first lock only after it gets the second.

That is a deadlock: a set of threads where each one waits for something another one in the set holds. Nothing throws. Nothing logs. CPU use drops to zero, both threads sit in BLOCKED, and every request that needs either account joins the queue behind them. In a payment service, the first sign is usually a health check that times out and a pool with no free threads.

The nasty part is timing. The bad interleaving needs both threads to take their first lock inside the same tiny window. A test that runs one transfer at a time never sees it. Under load, with thousands of transfers a second between the same busy merchant accounts, it is only a matter of when.

The simulator lets you play the scheduler. Run T1 to the end, then T2, and both transfers finish. Then reset and give each thread one step first.

sim.title: Two transfers, two locks, opposite orders
sim.intro: T1 runs transfer(a, b), T2 runs transfer(b, a). First let them finish one after the other. Then reset and find the order that freezes both.

goal.say: Both transfers finished. Now reset and give each thread its first lock before either takes its second.

try.title: Freeze two transfers
steps: Read DeadlockDemo. Each thread takes its first lock, sleeps 300 ms, then asks for the second.
Run it. After one second, main asks the JVM which threads are deadlocked.
Delete the sleep(300) line and run it a few times. Does it still deadlock every time?

code.title: DeadlockDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l06; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; import java.lang.management.ThreadInfo; import java.lang.management.ThreadMXBean; /** Two transfers lock the same two accounts in opposite orders. Run with -Pargs=wait to keep it alive for jcmd. */ public class DeadlockDemo { static final Object accountA = new Object(); static final Object accountB = new Object(); public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { boolean stayAlive = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("wait"); Thread t1 = new Thread(() -> move(accountA, accountB), "transfer-A-to-B"); Thread t2 = new Thread(() -> move(accountB, accountA), "transfer-B-to-A"); t1.setDaemon(true); // daemon, so the JVM can still exit at the end t2.setDaemon(true); t1.start(); t2.start(); Thread.sleep(1_000); ThreadMXBean mx = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean(); long[] ids = mx.findDeadlockedThreads(); // what a health check can ask the JVM System.out.println("deadlocked threads: " + (ids == null ? 0 : ids.length)); if (ids != null) { for (ThreadInfo info : mx.getThreadInfo(ids)) { System.out.println(" " + info.getThreadName() + " is " + info.getThreadState() + ", wants a lock held by " + info.getLockOwnerName()); } } if (stayAlive) { System.out.println("pid " + ProcessHandle.current().pid() + ": run jcmd " + ProcessHandle.current().pid() + " Thread.print in another terminal (60 s)"); Thread.sleep(60_000); } } static void move(Object from, Object to) { synchronized (from) { sleep(300); // widen the window: the other thread takes its first lock now synchronized (to) { System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName() + " moved the money"); } } } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } }

alt.title: DeadlockDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l06 import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory // Two transfers lock the same two accounts in opposite orders. Run with -Pargs=wait to keep it alive for jcmd. private val accountA = Any() private val accountB = Any() fun main(args: Array<String>) { val stayAlive = args.firstOrNull() == "wait" val t1 = Thread({ move(accountA, accountB) }, "transfer-A-to-B").apply { isDaemon = true; start() } val t2 = Thread({ move(accountB, accountA) }, "transfer-B-to-A").apply { isDaemon = true; start() } Thread.sleep(1_000) val mx = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean() val ids = mx.findDeadlockedThreads() // what a health check can ask the JVM println("deadlocked threads: ${ids?.size ?: 0}") ids?.let { mx.getThreadInfo(it) }?.forEach { info -> println(" ${info.threadName} is ${info.threadState}, wants a lock held by ${info.lockOwnerName}") } if (stayAlive) { val pid = ProcessHandle.current().pid() println("pid $pid: run jcmd $pid Thread.print in another terminal (60 s)") Thread.sleep(60_000) } } private fun move(from: Any, to: Any) { synchronized(from) { Thread.sleep(300) // widen the window: the other thread takes its first lock now synchronized(to) { println("${Thread.currentThread().name} moved the money") } } }

try.expect: With the sleep: deadlocked threads: 2, both BLOCKED, each waiting for a lock the other holds, and neither "moved the money" line. Without the sleep it deadlocks only sometimes, and often both transfers finish. That is the same bug, now hiding. The sleep only widens a window that is always there.

video.title: Two locks taken in opposite orders: the wait-for cycle, and one global lock order that breaks it

sections.h: Deadlock needs four conditions, so break one
sections.html:
A deadlock can only happen when all four of these hold at once. They are known as the Coffman conditions, after a 1971 paper.

  1. Mutual exclusion. A resource can be held by only one thread at a time. A lock is exactly that.
  2. Hold and wait. A thread holds one resource while it waits for another.
  3. No preemption. Nobody can take a resource away from the thread that holds it. It has to let go on its own.
  4. Circular wait. There is a cycle: T1 waits for T2, which waits for T1. Longer cycles count too.

Remove any one and deadlock becomes impossible. In practice you pick from three moves.

Break circular wait with a global lock order. If every thread that needs both a and b takes them in the same order, no thread can hold the second while waiting for the first, so no cycle can form. This is the fix you'll reach for most often, and the next section shows it.

Break no-preemption with a timed tryLock. A thread that can't get its second lock in time gives back the first and tries again later. It preempts itself.

Break hold-and-wait by needing only one lock: one coarse lock around both accounts, or an operation designed so it never holds one resource while asking for another.

Mutual exclusion is the one you rarely remove, since it is the reason you took a lock. Sometimes you can design it away, with immutable data or one owner per account (lesson 11 of this track).

The same four conditions apply to every kind of resource, not just Java locks: database row locks, connections from a pool, permits from a semaphore. The figure shows the cycle from the first section as a wait-for graph. Deadlock detectors, including the JVM's, look for exactly this loop.

Test the model on a case with no Java locks. A pool has 20 database connections. Twenty request threads each hold one and ask the pool for a second. Which of the four conditions hold, and which move would you pick? (All four: a connection serves one thread, each thread holds one while it waits, the pool can't take one back, and every thread waits for a connection that another thread holds. Taking one connection per request breaks hold and wait. A timeout on the second, after which the thread gives back its first, breaks no preemption.)

sections.h: Fix it with a global lock order
sections.html:
Give every account a stable, unique key, and always lock the lower key first, whichever way the money moves:

Java
void transfer(Account from, Account to, long cents) {
    Account first = from.id() < to.id() ? from : to;   // one order for everyone
    Account second = first == from ? to : from;
    synchronized (first) {
        synchronized (second) {
            from.debit(cents);
            to.credit(cents);
        }
    }
}
Kotlin
fun transfer(from: Account, to: Account, cents: Long) {
    val first = if (from.id < to.id) from else to      // one order for everyone
    val second = if (first === from) to else from
    synchronized(first) {
        synchronized(second) {
            from.debit(cents)
            to.credit(cents)
        }
    }
}

Now transfer(a, b) and transfer(b, a) both lock a first. Whoever gets a gets to run. The other waits for a while holding nothing, which is plain contention, not deadlock.

Three details make or break this.

The key must be unique and must never change. An account id or an IBAN works. hashCode() does not: two different objects can share one, and then two threads may again disagree about the order. If you have no natural key, Java Concurrency in Practice shows a tie-breaker: compare System.identityHashCode, and on a tie take one extra global lock first.

The rule must be global. Each method locking in a sensible-looking order is not enough. One method that locks account then customer, and another that locks customer then account, recreate the cycle. Put the ordering in one helper and make every caller use it.

The order must survive calls you don't see. If you call a listener, a repository or any other alien code while you hold a lock, that code may take locks of its own in a different order. That is the rule from lesson 4 of this track again: copy what you need, release the lock, then call out.

In the lab, Account has a ReentrantLock instead of using synchronized, so that part 2 can use tryLock. The ordering idea is the same.

try.title: Same transfers, one order
steps: Read OrderedLocks. It runs 100,000 transfers in each direction between the same two accounts, with the ordering rule above.
Predict whether it finishes, then run it.
Break it on purpose: change move to lock from first and to second. Run it again, and stop it with Ctrl+C if it hangs.

code.title: OrderedLocks.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l06; /** The same opposite transfers, with every thread taking the locks in one global order. */ public class OrderedLocks { record Acct(int id, long[] balance) {} public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Acct a = new Acct(1, new long[] {1_000_000}); Acct b = new Acct(2, new long[] {1_000_000}); Thread t1 = new Thread(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) move(a, b, 1); }, "A-to-B"); Thread t2 = new Thread(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) move(b, a, 1); }, "B-to-A"); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); t1.start(); t2.start(); t1.join(); t2.join(); System.out.printf("200,000 opposite transfers in %d ms, total still %,d%n", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, a.balance()[0] + b.balance()[0]); } static void move(Acct from, Acct to, long cents) { Acct first = from.id() < to.id() ? from : to; // lower id first, whatever the direction Acct second = first == from ? to : from; synchronized (first) { synchronized (second) { from.balance()[0] -= cents; to.balance()[0] += cents; } } } }

alt.title: OrderedLocks.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l06 import kotlin.concurrent.thread // The same opposite transfers, with every thread taking the locks in one global order. private class Acct(val id: Int, var balance: Long) fun main() { val a = Acct(1, 1_000_000) val b = Acct(2, 1_000_000) val t0 = System.nanoTime() val t1 = thread(name = "A-to-B") { repeat(100_000) { move(a, b, 1) } } val t2 = thread(name = "B-to-A") { repeat(100_000) { move(b, a, 1) } } t1.join() t2.join() println("200,000 opposite transfers in %d ms, total still %,d" .format((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, a.balance + b.balance)) } private fun move(from: Acct, to: Acct, cents: Long) { val first = if (from.id < to.id) from else to // lower id first, whatever the direction val second = if (first === from) to else from synchronized(first) { synchronized(second) { from.balance -= cents to.balance += cents } } }

try.expect: With ordered locks, 200,000 opposite transfers finish in well under a second and the total stays 2,000,000. Locking in argument order usually hangs within the first few thousand transfers. With no sleep to widen the window, it is down to luck, so on some runs it may survive a while.

sections.h: Timed tryLock, and the livelock it can cause
sections.html:
Sometimes you can't impose an order, for example when you don't know all the locks up front. Then make sure no wait can last forever. ReentrantLock.tryLock(timeout) gives up after the timeout and returns false. If you can't get both locks, let go of what you hold, wait a little, and try again:

Java
if (from.lock().tryLock(10, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) {
    try {
        if (to.lock().tryLock(10, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) {
            try { /* move the money */ return true; }
            finally { to.lock().unlock(); }
        }
    } finally {
        from.lock().unlock();      // couldn't get both: let go of everything
    }
}
Thread.sleep(ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextLong(1, 10));   // random back-off, then retry
Kotlin
if (from.lock().tryLock(10, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) {
    try {
        if (to.lock().tryLock(10, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) {
            try { /* move the money */ return true }
            finally { to.lock().unlock() }
        }
    } finally {
        from.lock().unlock()       // couldn't get both: let go of everything
    }
}
Thread.sleep(ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextLong(1, 10))    // random back-off, then retry

The random back-off matters more than it looks. Leave it out, or use a fixed sleep, and two threads can fall into lockstep: both take their first lock, both fail on the second, both release, both retry at the same moment, forever. That is livelock. The threads are busy, they change state all the time, and nothing gets done. A thread dump looks healthy, which makes livelock harder to spot than deadlock.

The demo below shows a livelock with no locks at all. Two polite diners share one spoon, and each hands it over whenever the other is hungry. In one second they pass it about ten million times and nobody eats. The fix is to break the symmetry: random back-off, or a rule such as "after three polite turns, eat anyway".

The third failure is starvation: the system makes progress, but one thread never does. A non-fair ReentrantLock (the default) lets a thread that just released the lock grab it again before a waiter wakes up. That is faster overall, but one unlucky thread can wait a long time. new ReentrantLock(true) hands the lock to the longest waiter instead. It costs throughput, and its Javadoc warns that fairness of locks does not guarantee fairness of thread scheduling. Starvation also happens when readers keep a read-write lock busy so a writer never gets in. Lesson 12 of this track comes back to that.

try.title: Watch a livelock, then break the symmetry
steps: Run LivelockDemo. Both diners are hungry and both are polite.
Read the count of handovers and meals.
Run it again with -Pargs=fixed, where a diner eats anyway after three polite turns.

code.title: LivelockDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l06; /** Two polite diners share one spoon. Each hands it over while the other is hungry. Try -Pargs=fixed. */ public class LivelockDemo { static volatile int spoonOwner = 0; // diner 0 or diner 1 static final boolean[] hungry = {true, true}; // written by its owner only, read by the other static volatile boolean stop; static final long[] handovers = new long[2]; public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { boolean fixed = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("fixed"); Thread d0 = new Thread(() -> dine(0, fixed), "diner-0"); Thread d1 = new Thread(() -> dine(1, fixed), "diner-1"); d0.start(); d1.start(); d0.join(1_000); d1.join(1_000); stop = true; d0.join(); d1.join(); System.out.printf("spoon handed over %,d times; meals eaten: %d%n", handovers[0] + handovers[1], (hungry[0] ? 0 : 1) + (hungry[1] ? 0 : 1)); } static void dine(int me, boolean fixed) { int other = 1 - me; int politeTurns = 0; while (!stop) { if (spoonOwner != me) { // not my spoon: wait for it Thread.onSpinWait(); continue; } boolean otherHungry; synchronized (hungry) { otherHungry = hungry[other]; } if (otherHungry && (!fixed || politeTurns < 3)) { politeTurns++; handovers[me]++; spoonOwner = other; // "you first": both keep saying it continue; } synchronized (hungry) { hungry[me] = false; } // eat spoonOwner = other; // then pass the spoon on return; } } }

alt.title: LivelockDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l06 import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Two polite diners share one spoon. Each hands it over while the other is hungry. Try -Pargs=fixed. @Volatile private var spoonOwner = 0 // diner 0 or diner 1 private val hungry = booleanArrayOf(true, true) // guarded by synchronized(hungry) @Volatile private var stop = false private val handovers = LongArray(2) fun main(args: Array<String>) { val fixed = args.firstOrNull() == "fixed" val d0 = thread(name = "diner-0") { dine(0, fixed) } val d1 = thread(name = "diner-1") { dine(1, fixed) } d0.join(1_000) d1.join(1_000) stop = true d0.join() d1.join() val meals = (if (hungry[0]) 0 else 1) + (if (hungry[1]) 0 else 1) println("spoon handed over %,d times; meals eaten: %d".format(handovers[0] + handovers[1], meals)) } private fun dine(me: Int, fixed: Boolean) { val other = 1 - me var politeTurns = 0 while (!stop) { if (spoonOwner != me) { // not my spoon: wait for it Thread.onSpinWait() continue } val otherHungry = synchronized(hungry) { hungry[other] } if (otherHungry && (!fixed || politeTurns < 3)) { politeTurns++ handovers[me]++ spoonOwner = other // "you first": both keep saying it continue } synchronized(hungry) { hungry[me] = false } // eat spoonOwner = other // then pass the spoon on return } }

try.expect: Without the fix: around ten million handovers in one second and meals eaten: 0. Both threads were RUNNABLE the whole time. With -Pargs=fixed: 6 handovers and 2 meals, done at once.

sections.h: Read a deadlock from a thread dump
sections.html:
When a service freezes, take a thread dump before you restart it. The restart destroys the evidence.

jcmd                      # lists Java processes with their PIDs
jcmd <pid> Thread.print   # every thread's state and stack, plus deadlock detection

jstack <pid> prints the same dump. If the JVM finds a cycle of threads waiting for each other's locks, it says so at the end. This is real output from the demo, on JDK 21:

Found one Java-level deadlock:
=============================
"transfer-A-to-B":
  waiting to lock monitor 0x00007f70d4001870 (object 0x00000006f794b518, a java.lang.Object),
  which is held by "transfer-B-to-A"

"transfer-B-to-A":
  waiting to lock monitor 0x00007f70d80012f0 (object 0x00000006f794b508, a java.lang.Object),
  which is held by "transfer-A-to-B"

Java stack information for the threads listed above:
===================================================
"transfer-A-to-B":
	at workbench.concurrency.l06.DeadlockDemo.move(DeadlockDemo.java:42)
	- waiting to lock <0x00000006f794b518> (a java.lang.Object)
	- locked <0x00000006f794b508> (a java.lang.Object)
	...
Found 1 deadlock.

Read it from the bottom up. Each thread's stack shows what it holds (- locked <...>) and what it wants (- waiting to lock <...>), and the header names the owner of the lock it wants. The line numbers take you straight to the two synchronized blocks that lock in opposite orders.

The detector also finds deadlocks on ReentrantLock. Then the dump says waiting for ownable synchronizer ... which is held by, and the stack shows parking to wait for instead of waiting to lock. Add -l (Thread.print -l) to list the java.util.concurrent locks each thread owns.

For tooling, jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json dump.json writes JSON. On JDK 21 each thread has only tid, name and stack. From JDK 25 it also has state, blockedOn, waitingOn, owner and the monitors each thread holds, which is enough to rebuild the wait-for graph.

Inside the process you can ask the same question in code, which makes a cheap health check:

Java
long[] ids = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean().findDeadlockedThreads();   // null if none
Kotlin
val ids: LongArray? = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean().findDeadlockedThreads()   // null if none

Two limits to know. The detector only sees cycles of Java locks. Twenty threads that each hold a pooled database connection and wait for a second one are deadlocked too, but the dump just shows twenty threads waiting inside the pool. And there is no JFR event for deadlocks: you find them with thread dumps or ThreadMXBean.

try.title: Take the dump yourself
steps: Run ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l06.DeadlockDemo -Pargs=wait. It deadlocks, prints its PID, and stays alive for 60 seconds.
In a second terminal, run jcmd <pid> Thread.print with that PID. Find Found one Java-level deadlock and follow each thread's locked and waiting to lock lines to a line number.
Run jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json /tmp/dump.json and open the file. Which fields does each thread have on your JDK?

code.title: terminal 2
code.html: jcmd # find the PID of DeadlockDemo jcmd <pid> Thread.print jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json /tmp/dump.json

try.expect: The text dump ends with Found 1 deadlock. and points at DeadlockDemo.java:42 for both threads. The JSON has tid, name and stack per thread on JDK 21, and state and lock fields as well on JDK 25 and later. Thread.dump_to_file refuses to overwrite an existing file unless you add -overwrite.

refs.title: diagnosticCommand.hpp at jdk-27-ga: the jcmd Thread.* commands

analogy: Deadlock is two cars meeting head-on at a one-lane bridge: each waits for the other to back up, and neither will. Lock ordering is a rule that traffic always crosses from the north side first. Livelock is both drivers backing up at the same moment, then both driving forward again, over and over. Starvation is the car on a side road that never finds a gap in the traffic, while everyone else gets through. The analogy breaks in one useful way: real drivers eventually lose patience and do something different. Threads never do, unless you write the timeout and the random back-off into the code yourself.
world: You'll meet the same cycle outside the JVM. Two ledger transactions that run SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the same two account rows in opposite orders deadlock in Oracle. Oracle detects that, fails one statement with ORA-00060: deadlock detected while waiting for resource, and your service sees an exception. The fix is the one from this lesson: lock rows in id order, for example with a single SELECT ... WHERE id IN (...) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE. The other common one is pool deadlock: a Quarkus endpoint that takes a connection from a pool of 20, then calls a method that needs a second connection from the same pool. With 20 concurrent requests, every thread holds one connection and waits for another, forever. No Java lock is involved, so no detector will name it.
mistake: The most common real mistake is believing that each method's locking order is enough. Developers check that transfer always locks from then to and call it consistent, but "from first" is a different order for every pair of calls. The same trap appears across classes: OrderService locks the order then the customer, CustomerService locks the customer then the orders. The fix is one rule for the whole system, such as "lower id first", written once in a helper that every caller uses, plus a review rule that nothing calls alien code while holding a lock.

compare.title: Ordered locking in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Java
java.html: void transfer(Account from, Account to, long cents) { Account first = from.id() < to.id() ? from : to; Account second = first == from ? to : from; first.lock().lock(); try { second.lock().lock(); try { from.debit(cents); to.credit(cents); } finally { second.lock().unlock(); } } finally { first.lock().unlock(); } }

kotlin.title: Kotlin
kotlin.html: fun transfer(from: Account, to: Account, cents: Long) { val first = if (from.id < to.id) from else to val second = if (first === from) to else from first.lock().withLock { // kotlin.concurrent.withLock: lock, try, finally unlock second.lock().withLock { from.debit(cents) to.credit(cents) } } }

compare.note: The idea is identical, and so is the deadlock risk: Kotlin adds no protection here. What differs is ceremony. Kotlin's withLock { } extension on Lock writes the lock(), try, finally unlock() for you, so you can't forget the finally. In Java the try/finally pairs are on you, and an unlock() in the wrong finally is a classic way to leak a lock. Both languages get the same dump from jcmd, since Kotlin compiles to the same ReentrantLock and monitor calls.

worked.title: Find a deadlock that hides behind a callback

steps.say: A ledger tells an audit log about every posting. A scheduler flushes the audit log every second, and the flush reads the ledger's balance. Each class looks fine on its own. Find the cycle.
steps.code: class Ledger { synchronized void post(Entry e) { entries.add(e); auditLog.record(e); // calls AuditLog while holding the Ledger lock } synchronized long balance() { return sum(entries); } } class AuditLog { synchronized void record(Entry e) { pending.add(e); } synchronized void flush() { long b = ledger.balance(); // calls Ledger while holding the AuditLog lock write(pending, b); pending.clear(); } }

alt.html: class Ledger(private val auditLog: AuditLog) { @Synchronized fun post(e: Entry) { entries += e auditLog.record(e) // calls AuditLog while holding the Ledger lock } @Synchronized fun balance(): Long = sum(entries) } class AuditLog { @Synchronized fun record(e: Entry) { pending += e } @Synchronized fun flush() { val b = ledger.balance() // calls Ledger while holding the AuditLog lock write(pending, b) pending.clear() } }

steps.say: A request thread in post holds the Ledger lock and wants the AuditLog lock. The scheduler thread in flush holds the AuditLog lock and wants the Ledger lock. That is the AB/BA cycle again, split across two classes. The dump would show it like this:
steps.code:
"http-worker-7":  waiting to lock <0x...a0> (a AuditLog), locked <0x...b8> (a Ledger)
"audit-flusher":  waiting to lock <0x...b8> (a Ledger),   locked <0x...a0> (a AuditLog)

steps.say: You could impose an order, but the cleaner fix is to stop holding a lock while calling the other class. Each method keeps its own lock only around its own state. Before reading the fix, decide: which call in each method is the alien one?
steps.code: void post(Entry e) { synchronized (this) { entries.add(e); } auditLog.record(e); // 1. no Ledger lock held while calling out } void flush() { long b = ledger.balance(); // 2. read the balance before taking our own lock List<Entry> batch; synchronized (this) { batch = List.copyOf(pending); pending.clear(); } write(batch, b); // 3. slow I/O with no lock at all }

alt.html: fun post(e: Entry) { synchronized(this) { entries += e } auditLog.record(e) // 1. no Ledger lock held while calling out } fun flush() { val b = ledger.balance() // 2. read the balance before taking our own lock val batch = synchronized(this) { pending.toList().also { pending.clear() } } write(batch, b) // 3. slow I/O with no lock at all }

steps.say: Now no thread ever holds one of the two locks while asking for the other, so hold-and-wait is gone and no cycle can form. The balance written with the batch may be a moment older than the last entry. For an audit log that is fine; if it weren't, you'd need one lock over both, which is the coarse-lock fix.

lab.title: Fix a transfer deadlock, then add a transfer that gives up
steps: Run the tests. Two transfer tests time out after 10 seconds: they deadlocked. The three tryTransfer tests fail with UnsupportedOperationException.
Read Account. You don't change it. debit and credit throw unless you hold that account's lock.
Part 1: fix Transfers.transfer so it always locks the account with the lower id() first. Keep the try/finally around each unlock().

Part 2: write tryTransfer. Loop until the deadline: tryLock the first account for 10 ms, then the second for 10 ms. If you get both, move the money and return true. If not, release what you hold, sleep a random 1 to 10 ms, and loop. Return false when time is up.
Run the tests until all five pass, then run them twice more.
hints: A self-transfer (from == to) takes the same ReentrantLock twice. That is fine, because it is reentrant, as long as you release it twice.
In part 2, put the from.lock().unlock() in a finally that runs whether or not you got to. The test checks that from is free after a failed attempt.
ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextLong(1, 10) gives a random back-off without sharing a Random between threads.
lab.done: All five tests in TransfersTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: Ordered locking from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write transfer(Account from, Account to, long cents) using each account's ReentrantLock, so that two transfers in opposite directions can never deadlock. Check: does every lock() have its unlock() in a finally?

answer.html: void transfer(Account from, Account to, long cents) { Account first = from.id() < to.id() ? from : to; Account second = first == from ? to : from; first.lock().lock(); try { second.lock().lock(); try { from.debit(cents); to.credit(cents); } finally { second.lock().unlock(); } } finally { first.lock().unlock(); } }

alt.title: Kotlin
alt.html: fun transfer(from: Account, to: Account, cents: Long) { val first = if (from.id < to.id) from else to val second = if (first === from) to else from first.lock().lock() try { second.lock().lock() try { from.debit(cents) to.credit(cents) } finally { second.lock().unlock() } } finally { first.lock().unlock() } }

recap: Deadlock needs all four conditions: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait. Break any one.
The usual fix is a global lock order by a unique, stable key, written once and used everywhere.
Timed tryLock with release and random back-off ensures no wait lasts forever. Without the randomness you can get livelock.
Livelock is busy threads making no progress. Starvation is one thread that never gets its turn while others do.
jcmd <pid> Thread.print (or jstack) reports Java-level deadlocks on monitors and on ReentrantLock, with the holder and the waiter.
Calling alien code while holding a lock is the most common way a cycle sneaks in across classes.

explain.prompt: A teammate says: "We added tryLock(5, SECONDS) everywhere, so we can't have deadlocks any more." Explain what they got right, and what can still go wrong.
explain.answer: They're right that a timed tryLock means no thread waits forever, so the classic deadlock can't freeze the system: a thread that can't get its second lock gives up after the timeout. But giving up only helps if the code then releases what it holds and tries again later, ideally after a random back-off. If two threads retry in lockstep, they can livelock, failing over and over. A 5-second timeout also means a request can stall for 5 seconds before it even notices. Lock ordering removes the cycle altogether, so I'd use that where we can, and keep timed tryLock for the cases where we can't know the order.

deeper.html:
The JVM's detector covers two kinds of lock. ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads() looks for cycles on monitors and on ownable synchronizers such as ReentrantLock and the write lock of ReentrantReadWriteLock. The older findMonitorDeadlockedThreads() sees monitors only. Neither sees semaphores, latches, Object.wait(), futures waiting on each other or pooled connections, because none of those has a single owning thread the JVM could point at.

That covers the common case of two thread pools waiting on each other. Task A runs on pool 1 and blocks on a Future from pool 2, while pool 2's only thread is blocked on a Future from pool 1. No lock is involved, so the detector stays silent. The dump still gives it away if you read the stacks: every pool thread is parked in FutureTask.get or CompletableFuture.join. Java Concurrency in Practice calls this thread-starvation deadlock.

JSON thread dumps keep improving. JDK 25 added per-thread state, parkBlocker, blockedOn, waitingOn, owner and the monitors each thread owns. JDK 26 added java.util.concurrent lock information. JDK 27 added a formatVersion field. If you build tooling on these dumps, check that field and the JDK version first.

Databases take the opposite approach to the JVM. Oracle detects deadlocks between sessions and breaks them by failing one statement. Your code must be ready to retry that transaction, ideally after ordering its row locks so the retry doesn't deadlock again.
